findings.title: Final answer in alternate box command ignored; earlier \boxed draft graded
findings.mechanism: The response puts a correct-looking draft in \boxed{} and then gives its real, different final answer in an equivalent box command such as \fbox{}. The parser searches only for the literal \boxed token, so it skips the later box and grades the abandoned draft, which matches gold.
findings.preconditions: Applies to graders that extract the answer from the last \boxed{...} (or another single fixed marker) by literal string search and then compare it to gold, while the model is free to emit other LaTeX.
findings.defense: Tokenize every LaTeX box-like command (\fbox, \framebox, \boxed, \colorbox, etc.) and treat the last one of any kind as the final answer. If it is not an accepted form, or the boxes conflict, award zero. Normalize wrappers, case and whitespace so legitimate answers still match.

findings.defense: Tokenize every backslash command, allowing optional whitespace before the argument and covering all box-like macros. Require the final box command to be a plain \boxed or \fbox at brace depth 0 with a cleanly brace-matched argument that contains no nested box. Give zero credit when the true last box is ambiguous, nested, or of an unrecognized type, then compare the normalized content to gold.

findings.title: Escaped-brace desync hides a decoy final box inside an earlier open box
findings.mechanism: The response opens one box containing a wrong label and an escaped brace, then later writes a second box with the gold label and a stray closing brace. A grader that finds the last box by string search (or skips escaped braces) reads the trailing box as a clean top-level final answer. A naive brace counter instead sees it nested inside the first, unclosed box, so the real committed answer is ambiguous or wrong.
findings.preconditions: This applies to graders that pull the final answer from the last \boxed{...} through rfind or a brace matcher, where the output may contain escaped braces or several boxes. It matters most for multiple-choice tasks, where hedging between labels is cheap.
findings.defense: Parse brace depth both with and without escape handling and reject the response if they disagree about box boundaries or top-level depth. Also reject any escaped brace inside or around a box, and any response with more than one distinct boxed answer. Give credit only when exactly one top-level box holds a single normalized label that matches gold.

findings.title: First-letter extraction ignores final answer marker; exotic whitespace hides mar
findings.mechanism: The original extractor returns the first standalone A-E letter in the response, so a stray leading letter earns credit even when a later explicit 'Answer: X' line names a different choice. The response can also write a further answer marker using control characters such as U+001F as separators. A whitespace class that counts these characters as whitespace reads that marker as real, while a stricter verifier does not.
findings.preconditions: This applies to multiple-choice graders that pull a single letter with a loose regex or a 'first match' heuristic. It also applies to any marker pattern that uses \s* in Python re, where non-printing control characters can act as separators.
findings.defense: Parse only the last explicit answer marker and require a standalone valid letter right after it. Define separators as an explicit set such as [ \t] or Unicode White_Space, or strip or normalize control and format characters first. Reject responses whose answer markers disagree with each other, and accept bare letters only when the whole response is just the letter.
